technical: The opening presents a finding the lab did not isolate. It compares agent console output from a local Docker check with spans read from Splunk in a separate EKS run, then concludes that the Collector or Splunk APM added the keys. Different environment, different run, and no reading taken at the Collector. Fix: In the EKS run, add a debug or file exporter to the Collector's traces pipeline. Print the database keys on the same default-pair trace as the Collector receives them and as it exports them, next to the Splunk APM read. Then say which layer adds them. Until then, move this point out of the opening into the body and label it as an observation.

technical: The claim about the database node name rests on screenshots from an earlier run that stopped early. Nothing in the reported run measures it. Fix: Take screenshots of the run whose numbers the post reports. Also have fix.sh read the inferred database node or service name for each pair from the APM API and print it to 05-fix.log, then cite that line.

editorial: A checklist item tells readers to build new searches on keys whose source in the pipeline was not established. If their Collector or APM setup does not add these keys to 2.x spans, the searches will not match 2.x spans. Fix: Once the Collector capture above shows which layer adds the keys, name the Collector version or APM behaviour responsible and state the condition, for example "with Splunk OTel Collector chart 0.163.1". Otherwise, recommend these keys only after the reader confirms them on a 2.x span in their own org.

editorial: The step timings disagree with the lab's own README. That undermines the 'run it in your account' promise and its cost planning. Fix: Quote the measured terraform apply duration from the run log, and make the README and the post use the same figure.

The core contract holds. Both pairs had the same jar, the same node and the same load (19.89 rps, 0 errors). In each service, 65 pool series used the new names and 0 used the old ones. The use_time ratio was 989.4, 1009.7 and 992.5 across the three rounds, which matches ms to s.

The opening's second finding says db.query.text and db.system.name are added after the agent. It comes from comparing two different setups: a Docker console-exporter check and an EKS run read through the Collector and Splunk. The post admits the lab cannot tell whether the Collector or APM added them.
The claim about the postgresql:postgres|postgres database node comes from screenshots of an earlier run that stopped early. No measurement in the reported run checks it.
The span key measurements (span_db_keys, preview_old_span_keys) are self-reported in the evidence report. The pool series and load measurements are corroborated.
The reader is clear: a platform engineer deciding what to rename and convert. The checklist at the end is something they can act on.

The ~1000x use_time ratio confirms the ms-to-s change the OpenTelemetry blog already documents. The value a senior reader gets beyond the docs is the db.namespace value change and the extra keys on 2.x spans in Splunk, and the second of those is not isolated.
It is honest about what was not tested: wait_time and create_time units, dual emission, and the chart scaling it suggests but did not build.
Some passages read as generated: the TL;DR repeats the body, and the sentence lengths are very even. The session blocks look real enough.
There is no demand data. The brief rates demand as weak and cites only the OpenTelemetry blog's call to preview 3.0. No search volume, reactions or views were found.
It is timely, because 3.0 is coming and the project is asking users to test now. The headline uses the words a reader would search for: OTel Java agent 3.0, preview, pool metrics, DB spans.
It credits Splunk and OpenTelemetry with the answer and keeps a positive tone. Splunk fits naturally here, not forced.

claims.text: The OpenTelemetry project shipped 2.32.0 as the 3.0 release candidate and asks users to preview it now
The preview turns off dual emission for these names
The preview can still change before 3.0
The blog lists code and messaging renames as well
Agent release v2.33.1 is the version used
db.query.text, db.system.name, db.namespace, db.operation.name and db.collection.name on default spans are added after the agent, by the Collector or by Splunk APM
db.query.text and db.system.name are the safest keys for new searches

brief.reader: Platform engineer running Java services on Kubernetes with the OTel Java agent and Splunk Observability Cloud
brief.decision: What to rename and convert in Splunk before the agent's 3.0 defaults arrive: pool metric names, pool timing units and database span keys
brief.question: What will OTel Java agent 3.0 change in the connection pool metrics and database spans I see in Splunk, and how can I see it before I upgrade?
brief.takeaway: One environment variable on the agent you already run shows 3.0's database names in Splunk today. Side by side with the default agent under the same load, the run shows which pool metrics and span keys get new names, and that the same pool timing is stored about 1000 times smaller because it is now in seconds, so any threshold written on the old values is worth checking.
brief.adds: The OpenTelemetry blog lists the renamed fields and the testing steps. This post runs both modes side by side on one live system and shows the result in Splunk: the pool metric names per service, the same pool timing stored in milliseconds and in seconds over three rounds, and every database key on real traces.
brief.open_question: With OTEL_INSTRUMENTATION_COMMON_V3_PREVIEW=true alone on the same jar, running next to the default agent under the same load on EKS, which pool metric names does Splunk store per service, does any old name or old span key remain, and what is the ratio of the stored connection use time means in each of three rounds?
tradeoffs: The preview turns off the /dup dual emission for database, code and messaging, so old and new names are not sent side by side while it is on
The same pool timing is stored in seconds after the change, so anything built on the old millisecond values needs converting
The 2.33.1 preview can still change before 3.0, as the OpenTelemetry blog says
This run measures database pool metrics and database spans only; code and messaging renames are not measured
The preview pair uses its own deployment.environment so Splunk keeps the pairs apart; that label is the only other difference in the agent options
